source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Keep factory alarm limits unchanged because only engineering staff may adjust them","B":"Disable individualized alarm settings because they increase clinically useful alarms","C":"Individualize alarm limits within policy so alarms remain meaningful and safe","D":"Individualize alarm limits only in critical care and never on other monitored units"}}
source_row.rationale: Individualizing alarm parameters based on a specific client's baseline and clinical condition (within appropriate, safe limits and per facility policy) helps ensure alarms are clinically meaningful for that client, which can help reduce alarm fatigue from non-actionable alarms while still maintaining an appropriate safety margin — an approach supported by national patient safety goals on alarm management.
source_row.source_detail: 2026 performance-goal framework replaces NPSGs; clinical alarm systems require safe management under organization policy; effective Jan 1, 2026, accessed 2026-08-14.
source_row.stem: A nurse adjusts a cardiac monitor's alarm parameters for a specific client based on their baseline vital signs and clinical condition, and a colleague assumes this task is reserved strictly for biomedical engineering staff rather than bedside nurses.
